questions.q: What actually changes when training a QNN with k parameters compared to the 1-parameter loop from the Chapter 2 lab?
options: The gradient step now needs 2k circuit evaluations (two shifts per parameter), and every parameter is updated simultaneously using its own piece of the gradient -- but the loop structure itself is identical
An entirely different optimization algorithm is required, unrelated to gradient descent
The parameter-shift rule no longer applies once there is more than one parameter
Multi-parameter circuits cannot be trained using any gradient-based method
questions.explain: The loop (evaluate, compute loss, compute gradient via parameter-shift, update) stays the same; only the number of circuit evaluations needed for the gradient scales to 2k, and all k parameters update together each step.

questions.q: For f(theta1, theta2) = cos(theta1) + sin(theta2) at theta1 = theta2 = pi/4, what is the parameter-shift gradient with respect to theta1?
options: Approximately -0.7071, matching the calculus derivative -sin(pi/4)
Approximately 0.7071, matching cos(pi/4) itself
Exactly 0
Approximately 1.4142, double the expected value
questions.explain: Shifting only theta1 by +-pi/2 while holding theta2 fixed and applying the shift rule to cos(theta1) gives approximately -0.7071, exactly matching the analytic derivative -sin(pi/4).

questions.q: What specific noise source exists in QNN training that classical ML training does NOT have?
options: Shot noise -- the expectation value measured on real or shot-based-simulated hardware is a statistical estimate from a finite number of circuit repetitions, not an exact number
Floating point rounding error, which only affects quantum computations
Learning rate decay, which is unique to quantum optimizers
Mini-batch sampling, which is exclusive to quantum machine learning
questions.explain: Shot noise comes from needing a finite number of circuit repetitions to estimate an expectation value -- an additional statistical noise source stacked on top of (and sometimes compounding) the barren-plateau gradient-vanishing problem, with no classical ML analogue.

questions.q: What does a loss curve that is completely flat from the very FIRST training iteration most likely indicate, per this lesson?
options: A likely barren plateau -- the gradient was never informative from the start, not that training 'finished early'
Perfect convergence to the global optimum on the first step
A bug in the loss function that always returns zero
An unusually high learning rate causing instant convergence
questions.explain: A flat loss curve from iteration 1 is a classic signature of a barren plateau (Lesson 8): the gradient is near-zero everywhere, so there was never a meaningful signal to follow, rather than training having already succeeded.

questions.q: A loss curve decreases steadily then suddenly spikes upward partway through training. What does this lesson suggest is the likely cause?
options: A learning rate that's too large for the local curvature of the loss landscape at that point
This pattern always indicates a hardware failure with no software explanation
This is always a sign of a barren plateau
This pattern can only occur with mini-batch training, never full-batch
questions.explain: A sudden upward spike after a period of decrease is a classic sign of overshooting due to too-large a learning rate relative to how sharply the loss landscape curves at that point in parameter space.
